title: The More You Automate, the Less You See: Hidden Pitfalls of AI Scientist Systems
titleEn: The paper points out that the AI scientist system has four types of failure modes, which are difficult to detect by looking only at the final paper.
summary: The paper identifies four potential failure modes in contemporary AI scientist systems: improper benchmark selection, data leakage, metric misuse, and post-hoc selection bias. The authors design controlled experiments to isolate each failure mode individually, and after evaluating two mainstream open-source AI scientist systems, they find multiple failures of varying severity that are easily overlooked in practice. The study also shows that obtaining trace logs and code of the full automated workflow is more effective at detecting such problems than only examining the final paper, so they recommend that journals and conferences require these materials to be submitted with AI-generated research during review, to ensure transparency, accountability, and reproducibility. This paper is a NeurIPS 2025 AI4Science Spotlight.

parts.text: Fully automated AI scientists can go from hypotheses to writing papers, but the internal process is rarely audited. The authors worry that improper benchmark selection, data leakage, metric misuse, and reporting only favorable results can harm integrity, so they conduct isolated diagnostics in ML/AI settings.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: The authors built synthetic SPR tasks, using confounded benchmarks, label noise, conflicting SWA/CWA, and test score swapping to isolate and test four defects. The targets were Agent Laboratory and The AI Scientist v2. They then used an LLM classifier to compare final papers against logs plus code.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Agent Laboratory often selects from the front of the list; with SOTA, v2 more often selects easy benchmarks. No predefined peeking was seen, but there is undisclosed subsampling or self-generated data, and after swapping test scores, the reward changes selection. With 20 examples per type including injected positives, Accuracy is 55.0% paper-only and 82.0% with logs and code.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors state that only four failure modes and two systems are covered; detection relies on controlled experiments and behaviors visible in logs, review manipulation was not examined, and extrapolation to other systems and non-ML domains should be cautious. SPR is the experimental task; default LLM names are not reported; some audit positives are constructed by injection.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: How Can Rhetoric Reward-Hack AI Reviewers? Dissecting Rhetorical Sensitivity in AI-Based Peer Review

title: Judge Reliability Harness: Stress Testing the Reliability of LLM Judges
titleEn: Researchers release Judge Reliability Harness, stress-testing LLM judge reliability
summary: The researchers release the open-source library Judge Reliability Harness for building validation suites to test the reliability of LLM judges. The tool generates reliability tests for a given benchmark dataset and judge configuration, evaluating binary judgment accuracy and ordinal scoring performance, covering free-form and agent task formats. The authors evaluate four frontier judges on four benchmarks covering safety, persuasion, abuse, and agent behavior, finding notable differences across models and perturbation types, with no judge consistently reliable across all benchmarks. Preliminary experiments show that simple text format changes, paraphrasing, verbosity changes, and flipping true labels in LLM answers affect the accuracy with which judges assess another model's task completion ability. The code is open-sourced, and the paper is accepted at the ICLR 2026 Agents in the Wild workshop.

parts.text: LLMs are used as judges or autograders in evaluations, but model, rubric, and prompt configurations are rarely measured systematically. Agreement with humans on a small validation set does not reveal performance under changes in format, rewriting, verbosity, or sampling parameters.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Given a benchmark and judge configuration, JRH generates label-flip, formatting, paraphrase, length, duplicate, ordinal-bucket, and agent transcript variants, optionally with human acceptance or modification, then computes the proportion of judge scores matching the target label.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Four judges are not equally stable across four benchmarks. The authors state that no judge is stable across all benchmarks, Persuade is more fragile than binary-classification benchmarks, and cross-judge means are lower on format tests except for Fortress. The authors state that Llama 4.1 Maverick 17B tends to be more stable, at a fraction of the cost of other judges.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The paper does not list limitations. It covers four judges and four benchmarks; the first three benchmarks have 10 items each, and AgentHarm has 16. It does not report confidence intervals, agreement with humans, or ordinal generation temperature.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: ContextLeak: Auditing Leakage in Private In-Context Learning Methods
titleEn: ContextLeak: Auditing Privacy Leakage in Private In-Context Learning
summary: The researchers propose ContextLeak, a framework for empirically measuring worst-case information leakage in in-context learning (ICL). The method uses canary insertion to embed uniquely identifiable tokens into sensitive datasets, and constructs targeted queries to detect whether they appear. The authors apply it to various private ICL techniques, including heuristic prompt defenses and differentially private methods with formal guarantees, and the results show that ContextLeak can reliably detect leakage in each method, and that leakage increases monotonically with the theoretical privacy budget. The analysis also shows that existing methods trade off poorly between privacy and utility, either fully leaking sensitive information or severely harming performance.

parts.text: ICL puts examples that may contain sensitive information into the prompt, and malicious users may still extract information from the output. Heuristic defenses provide no privacy guarantees against an adversary, and DP upper bounds may be too loose, lacking an audit of measured worst-case leakage.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: ContextLeak inserts an identifiable canary into the sensitive context with probability 0.5, and submits adversarial queries, judging whether the canary exists only based on the privatized output, thereby giving an empirical ε lower bound. The query templates can be further optimized with GEPA.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Audit RNM, ESA, and L0–L3 on Llama3.3-70b, Qwen2.5-72b, and GPT-4.1. The authors state that leakage increases with theoretical ε; prompt injection achieves near 50% audit accuracy on L3, while this audit shows full leakage. RNM utility stagnates after empirical ε of about 0.4.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors note that only single-round queries are evaluated, synthetic-data-type DP is not systematically covered, and the canary and query designs are not exhaustive. The main experimental models are three large models, with an additional three small models for ablation; the DP audit uses aggregated outputs rather than final outputs.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Jailbreak-AudioBench: In-Depth Evaluation and Analysis of Jailbreak Threats for Large Audio Language Models
titleEn: Jailbreak-AudioBench: A Jailbreak Evaluation Benchmark for Large Audio Language Models
summary: The researchers propose Jailbreak-AudioBench for systematically evaluating audio jailbreak threats to large audio language models (LALMs), comprising a toolbox, a curated dataset, and a benchmark. The toolbox supports text-to-audio and multiple editing techniques that inject hidden semantics into audio. The dataset provides explicit and implicit jailbreak audio samples in both original and edited forms. The authors evaluate several current advanced LALMs with this dataset, claim it establishes the most comprehensive audio-modality jailbreak benchmark to date, and hope to expose stronger jailbreak threats such as query-based audio editing, advancing LALM safety alignment and defense research.

parts.text: End-to-end LALMs directly perceive hidden semantics such as speaking rate, pitch, noise, accent, and emotion. The authors say text and visual jailbreak research is abundant, but audio jailbreak still lacks systematic evaluation, and such edits may bypass safety constraints.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Use gTTS to convert jailbreak text to audio, then apply edits for volume, speed, intonation, pitch, noise, accent, and emotion. Questions are divided into Explicit and Implicit; ASR requires Llama Guard 3 to judge harmful and exceed 50 words. Also query with 32 combinations, and prepend audio instructions that refuse harmful content to the samples.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: After editing, ASR relative to the original audio goes up and down. On Explicit Small, query-based composition raises SALMONN-7B's ASR from 31.6% to 85.1%, and Gemini-2.5-Flash from 8.1% to 49.4%. The authors state that prepended audio instructions lower ASR, but the remaining values are still high.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors note that Llama Guard 3 misclassifies repetition as success, and plan to change the metric and add natural speech. The evaluation covers 10 end-to-end models, one inference per sample; the closed-source main table uses small sets of 262/237 samples, and Figure 6/9 do not include these two closed-source models.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Easier to Mislead Than to Correct: Harmful and Beneficial Revision in LLM Conformity
titleEn: Study: LLMs in multi-agent systems are more easily misled by peer consensus than corrected by it
summary: The paper conducts a controlled study of conformity behavior in LLMs within multi-agent systems: the model answers a question, then sees simulated peer answers and gives a final answer, manipulating two social cues: consensus structure and peer authority labels. Across four open-weight models and seven QA datasets, unanimous peer agreement misleads originally correct models at a much higher rate than it corrects originally wrong answers; authority labels make models more likely to choose the endorsed answer, regardless of its correctness. The authors also find that general reasoning interventions like chain-of-thought and reflection cannot reliably reduce harmful revisions while preserving beneficial ones, and therefore recommend that multi-agent LLM systems should verify peer answers rather than simply aggregate them.

parts.text: In multi-agent settings, a model may abandon its own answer because peer answers agree. The authors aim to compare, in the same controlled setting, whether this influence corrects initial errors as strongly as it misleads initially correct ones.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: The model first answers multiple-choice questions independently, then re-answers after seeing six simulated peers. Cross consensus structure with authority labels, using mixed peers as the shared baseline for both types of revision, and additionally test CoT and reflect-then-revise.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Without authority, when aggregating four models, the harmful revision rate under all-wrong is 62.9% (mixed 15.6%), and the beneficial revision rate under all-correct is 51.5% (mixed 32.7%, Table 1). As the number of authoritative figures increases, revisions more often move toward the endorsed option, regardless of correctness. Neither of the two reasoning prompts can suppress only harmful revisions.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors note the limitations of using only multiple-choice questions and simulated peers rather than live conversations, and that self-rated confidence is not a calibrated probability; they plan to continue with live multi-agent settings and open-ended generation. The experiments use four open-source models, 2,500 multiple-choice questions, and three seeds, with correctness judged against the gold label.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: RedDiffuser: Auditing Multimodal Safety Failures in Vision-Language Models via Reinforced Diffusion
titleEn: RedDiffuser: Using reinforcement diffusion to generate visual inputs for auditing VLM multimodal safety failures
summary: The researchers propose RedDiffuser (RedDiff), a reinforcement-based framework that uses diffusion models to generate semantically coherent visual inputs for black-box safety testing, combining greedy prompt search with reinforcement optimization to mine high-risk multimodal inputs that expose potential safety failures in VLMs. The paper studies multimodal safety auditing under exposure to harmful contexts, i.e., whether VLMs can maintain safe behavior when partially harmful text is paired with visual contexts. Experiments on open-source and commercial VLMs show that failures under such contextual conditions are relatively common: on LLaVA, RedDiffuser increases the unsafe response rate by up to 10.69% on the original set and 8.91% on the held-out set, and transfers to Gemini and LLaMA-Vision. The authors state that these vulnerabilities persist under external safety guardrails, indicating that current system-level safety mechanisms are still insufficient for real-world multimodal risks.

parts.text: VLMs in open environments often face incomplete, ambiguous multimodal inputs. The authors argue that testing only explicit malicious instructions misses a risk: when partially toxic text is paired with visual context, can safety alignment still block harmful continuations.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: RedDiffuser: with text fixed, Gemini greedily searches image prompts, then DDPO fine-tunes the diffusion model. The reward is Detoxify toxicity score plus λ times BERTScore. The guardrail variant zeroes the toxicity reward for samples that fail the dual NSFW check.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: LLaVA main subset Detoxify Any*: text-only 58.01%, aligned (M) 68.70% (Table 1). Hold-out unaligned variant 79.45% (Table 2). On Gemini-1.5-flash, aligned (M) 81.33% (Table 3).
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The paper does not specifically discuss limitations. The target model is LLaVA-1.5-7B, and it is transferred to Gemini-1.5-flash and LLaMA-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct. The paper does not report the number of repetitions or human agreement.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Your "Pro" LLM Subscription May Actually Be "Free": Exposing Fingerprint Spoofing Risks in LLM Inference Services
titleEn: Your "Pro" LLM Subscription May Actually Be "Free": Exposing Fingerprint Spoofing Risks in LLM Inference Services

title: Willing but Unable: Separating Refusal from Capability in Code LLMs via Abliteration
titleEn: The study uses ablation to remove the refusal direction in code LLMs, separating refusal from generation capability.
summary: The paper proposes using abliteration (a low-rank weight editing method that orthogonally projects out the refusal direction in the residual stream) to remove refusals in safety-aligned code LLMs for injected vulnerability prompts, using Python and CWE-89 (SQL injection) as case studies. It tests PromSec and SafeCoder safety samples on Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct 3B, 7B, and 14B, repeating each condition three times. Results show refusal strongly depends on model scale and prompt context: 14B refuses 100% of prompts, 7B refuses 73% on PromSec but only 5% on SafeCoder, and 3B is largely not blocked. After abliteration, refusals drop to zero or near zero across scales, with syntactic validity maintained above 93%; injection rates remain capability-limited, at 88-97% for 14B, 89-90% for 7B, and 25-48% for 3B. The authors conclude that refusal can be separated from code generation capability.

parts.text: Learned vulnerability detection lacks clean labels. Starting from secure code and asking the model to inject a specified CWE can reduce open-ended annotation to binary confirmation, but instruction-tuned code LLMs refuse prompts that name a CWE.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Apply abliteration to Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct 3B, 7B, 14B, orthogonally projecting out the refusal direction in the residual stream. Generated outputs are adjudicated with CodeQL, Semgrep, Bandit plus two authors to determine whether they constitute CWE-89.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: 14B Base has 100.0% refusal on both datasets, and 7B Base has 73.3% on PromSec and 4.7% on SafeCoder. After ablation, refusal drops to 0% or 1.7%; injection rates are 25.0% and 48.0% for 3B, and 88.3% and 96.7% for 14B (Table I).
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors limit the scope to CWE-89, Python, and the Qwen2.5-Coder family; future work includes other CWEs, languages, model families, and whether detectors can generalize to real vulnerable code. Inference uses Q4_K_M, and FP16 was not systematically reproduced.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Memento 3: Model-Based Recursive Self-Improvement through Reflective Rulebooks
titleEn: Memento 3 proposes a rulebook-based recursive self-improvement method
summary: The paper proposes Memento 3, enabling frozen large language model agents to continuously learn an explicit world model through external memory. The agent maintains a natural language rulebook as persistent semantic memory, recording revisable hypotheses about environment dynamics, and compiles the rulebook into executable code for prediction and planning. Through a continuous loop of observation, reflection, rule revision, compilation, and verification, the agent uses prediction errors to improve both the rulebook and the code; updated code is accepted only when the LLM judges that the code faithfully reflects the rulebook and that cell-by-cell replay reproduces the observed state transitions. The authors view this process as a model-based path toward recursive self-improvement, with the underlying LLM kept fixed. A population-scale extension maintains multiple world models in parallel, sharing interaction evidence and using its predictions to guide exploration.

parts.text: With limited interaction, multiple world models can fit at the same time, yet they differ in predictions on unseen states. A frozen-parameter LLM still needs to revise explicit environment rules in order to plan in unfamiliar environments.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Code as Model treats the natural language rulebook as semantic memory and compiles it into executable code for prediction and planning. Prediction errors drive reflection, revision, compilation, and verification; accepting updates requires that the code be faithful to the rulebook and that replay reproduce observed transitions cell by cell. Multiple models can be maintained in parallel and share evidence.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: On 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, the single-model setting completes all, with average RHAE of 100.0 and total actions at 0.44 of the human count. On Pong, the learned controller wins 21:0 across three different starting positions, with no further LLM calls at execution time.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The paper does not specifically discuss limitations. The report covers single-model results on 25 public games, rulebook ablations on three games, and an N=2 population on wa30; the Pong controller is evaluated on three openings. The paper does not report the number of main experiment repetitions or the number of LLM calls for ARC-AGI-3 learning.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: You Changed Your Mind, The Model Didn't: Demystifying Intent in Multi-Turn Dialogue
titleEn: The paper proposes the Intent-Eval benchmark, revealing that models confuse rejected intents in multi-turn dialogue
summary: The paper finds that large language models in multi-turn tasks treat proposals the user has rejected or replaced as still-active requirements; even when the user's final intent is unchanged, task execution can be led astray. The authors propose Intent-Eval, a controlled benchmark covering tool operation, code, database, and math tasks. Models are fragile on both rejected proposals and replaced requirements, and accuracy drops deepen or persist as interaction continues. To address this, the authors propose Intent-OPSD, an on-policy self-distillation framework under decision conditions. Teacher and Student are initialized from the same model; the frozen Teacher provides active-intent supervision based on the complete task matched to the user's decisions, and the Student is trained to follow the active requirements reflecting user intent over the full dialogue.

parts.text: In multi-turn tasks, after the user proposes a change and then rejects or revises it, the model may still answer according to content that was mentioned. The authors argue that what was said needs to be distinguished from requirements still in effect; otherwise task execution can be led astray.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Intent-Eval turns the same source task into four multi-turn conditions: no insertion, clarification only, refused proposal, accepted proposal, with single-turn controls. Intent-OPSD's frozen teacher sees the full single-turn task matching the decision, and the student performs on-policy self-distillation on the full conversation with token-level JS divergence.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Across eight models, multi-turn Original drops 36.30 percentage points from single-turn, and Retained and Revised drop another 8.06 and 5.55 percentage points. Across ten models, 59.63% of new Retained errors contain invalidated content. Intent-OPSD is 10.81 percentage points higher than Base across four models.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors note that the benchmark changes only one requirement at a time, rejected changes remain hard to handle, and training still relies on complete task specifications. Experiments cover ten models and 414 source tasks across four domains; RQ4 compares Base and SFT on four models; judgments use domain validators, and the paper does not report statistical tests.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: ROK-FORTRESS: Measuring the Effect of Geopolitical Transcreation for National Security and Public Safety
titleEn: ROK-FORTRESS: Measuring the Impact of Geopolitical Rewriting on National Security and Public Safety Evaluations with an English-Korean Transcreation Matrix
summary: The researchers propose ROK-FORTRESS, a bilingual, culturally adversarial national security and public safety (NSPS) benchmark using the English–Korean language pair and US–Korean geopolitical axes as a case study, separating the effects of language and geopolitical context through a transcreation matrix. The matrix evaluates adversarial intent under controlled combinations of English and Korean, and US and Korean entities, institutions, and operational details; each adversarial prompt is paired with a dual-use benign control to quantify over-refusal, and responses are scored by a calibrated LLM-as-a-judge panel against expert-written, prompt-specific binary rubrics. In two-track testing of frontier models and Korean-optimized models, Korean variants show a consistent suppression effect; the interaction between geopolitical context and language varies by model, with Korean context further mitigating language-driven suppression in some models. A direct-request ablation stripping jailbreak wrappers shows a small but consistent decrement for closed-source models, while open-source models show larger, wrapper-dependent, and directionally opposite effects; the authors argue part of Korean suppression comes from prompt specialization rather than language-based safety alignment itself. The transcreation matrix approach is designed to generalize to other language–culture pairs.

parts.text: NSPS multilingual safety evaluations mostly use translation, leaving original scenarios and entities unchanged, so they cannot separate how language surface form and geopolitical grounding each change safety behavior.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: ROK-FORTRESS has 1,235 English–Korean tasks, combining English/Korean with US/Korean entities via a transfer-creation matrix, computing TRS with prompt-specific rubrics, and comparing direct requests with jailbreak-wrapped ones removed.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: The authors say Korean variants had lower TRS in most paired comparisons, with summary language decreasing by +10.21 percentage points and situational by +4.47. Under direct requests, closed-source models averaged a language decrease of +4.5 percentage points, while the five open-source models were −6.0.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors limit the empirical findings to the English-Korean and US-Korea axes, and list external validity for other language pairs as next steps. The main evaluation covers 14 models and 1,235 tasks; the paper does not report the number of repeated sampling per item.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: StyleBreak: Revealing Alignment Vulnerabilities in Large Audio-Language Models via Style-Aware Audio Jailbreak
titleEn: StyleBreak: Jailbreaking with Stylized Audio to Reveal Alignment Vulnerabilities in Large Audio Language Models
summary: The researchers propose StyleBreak, a style-aware audio jailbreak framework that systematically examines how human speech attributes affect the alignment robustness of large audio-language models (LAMs). The framework employs a two-stage style-aware transformation pipeline that perturbs both text content and audio to control linguistic, paralinguistic, and extralinguistic attributes, and designs a query-adaptive policy network to automatically search for adversarial styles, improving jailbreak exploration efficiency. Evaluations show that LAMs exhibit critical vulnerabilities under diverse human speech attributes, and StyleBreak improves attack effectiveness and efficiency across multiple attack paradigms, leading the authors to conclude that LAMs require more robust alignment. This work has been accepted by AAAI 2026.

parts.text: LAMs connect audio encoders to LLMs for speech interaction, but audio jailbreak research is scarce. Existing approaches mostly convert text jailbreaks into speech, or add noise, change pitch, or switch accents, without systematically examining whether attributes like emotion, age, and gender affect alignment.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: StyleBreak first uses GPT-4 to rewrite queries by emotion, then uses CosyVoice2-0.5B to synthesize speech based on a reference audio, with 70 style combinations. The multi-head policy samples by query, and the reward is the average of ARR, ASR, PV, and TS. The appendix provides rewriting templates.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: 200 training strategies, 50 comparisons against four baseline types, each repeated 5 times. The abstract states that within three queries ASR improves by 7.1%–22.3%, while Table 1 also shows metric decreases. After transferring to GPT-4o, the authors state ASR rises by 2.1% to 9.5%.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors plan to consider noise, multilingualism, and front-end processing differences later, and, due to the lack of public audio jailbreak defenses, intend to design and evaluate their own. The experiments cover four open-source LAMs plus GPT-4o and Gemini-2.5-flash; the paper does not report consistency with human judgment.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

What Do Safety-Aligned LLMs Learn From Mixed Compliance Demonstrations?
titleEn: Study: How safety-aligned LLMs learn from mixed compliance demonstrations
summary: The paper studies how models interpret different types of compliant demonstrations when benign compliant demonstrations (harmless requests plus helpful responses) and harmful compliant demonstrations (harmful requests plus helpful responses) are mixed in context. Across four models, the authors find that benign and harmful demonstrations are not interchangeable: benign demonstrations can either decrease or increase harmful compliance, depending on the specific model. The study further notes that preference optimization is the key training stage that prevents benign demonstrations from increasing harmful compliance, demonstration order exhibits a clear recency bias, and models differ in the relationship between refusal and in-context learning, with some adopting the demonstration format even when refusing, while others override all context signals when refusing. The authors state that this work advances from demonstrating that demonstration-based jailbreaks are effective to characterizing their operating mechanism: what a model extracts from compliant demonstrations depends on the demonstration content, order, and training method.

parts.text: Aligned models are sensitive to compliant demonstrations in context, but it is unclear whether they extract a general obedience signal or whether the demonstration request is harmful. The authors use a mix of benign and harmful compliant demonstrations to distinguish these two possibilities.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: The authors control the number of benign demonstrations Nb and harmful demonstrations Nh, use chi-square and logistic regression to test three count hypotheses, and compare OLMo's SFT, DPO, and Instruct checkpoints, additionally testing five orders and whether format adoption is independent of compliance.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: All four models reject the total-count hypothesis at some N. In Table 2, Llama and Gemma have negative β2, OLMo-Instruct does not reject the harmful-count hypothesis, and GPT-OSS-20B has β2 of +0.0319. The SFT checkpoint has β2 of +0.0919, and after DPO the harmful-count hypothesis cannot be rejected.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors state that the stage analysis was done only on OLMo, because most providers do not release intermediate checkpoints. Future directions include more model families, base models, and other safety algorithms, as well as using interpretability to explain dilution and amplification. The paper does not report WildGuard and human agreement.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: APEXA: Execution-Integrity Enforcement for Multi-Agent LLM Automation of Synchrotron Data Reduction
titleEn: APEXA adds execution integrity guardrails to LLM multi-agent systems for synchrotron data processing
summary: The paper proposes APEXA, a deployed framework that coordinates 61 tools for synchrotron data reduction and, through deterministic execution integrity guardrails, prevents returning results for tool calls that were not actually executed. The same tool layer also enforces motor safety constraints: over 50 adversarial scenarios and four models, it produced 0/200 violations against a simulated EPICS controller, versus 15/200 for the prompt-only baseline. The authors also release APEXA-Bench, containing 58 facility tasks organized by scientific correctness and physical consequence; on real APS beamline data, a single prompt recovered detector geometry and integrated a complete attenuation and exposure scan. The authors argue that trustworthy scientific agents require deterministic execution verification rather than model-side guarantees, and they release the framework, benchmark, and trajectories.

parts.text: Synchrotron data reduction is a multi-step expert process, and a language model's fluent reply does not mean the requested computation has been executed. Institutional gateways may also silently drop tool calls, and the model may still narrate calibrations that were not run.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: APEXA uses one reasoning agent to call 61 tools. A deterministic tool layer refuses to return results without an execution record and runs five checks before motor commands are issued. APEXA-BENCH contains 58 tasks labeled by four types of physical consequence.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: On 50 adversarial scenarios, four models, and a simulated EPICS IOC, tool-layer violations are 0/200, and the prompt-only baseline with roughly 700 tokens is 15/200. On APS 1-ID, one prompt completes calibration and integration, the detector distance in a CeO2 decay scan stays within ±0.02 mm, and non-physical calibrations are rejected.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The paper does not specifically discuss limitations. This paper reports motor safety gates and cross-detector task completion; large-scale scoring is left to the full paper, and the main text has no APEXA-Score. §IV-C only evaluates task completion, not refinement accuracy.

title: Echoes of Human Malice in Agents: Benchmarking LLMs for Multi-Turn Online Harassment Attacks
titleEn: The paper proposes a multi-turn online harassment agent benchmark; jailbreak fine-tuning raises the attack success rate above 95%
summary: The paper proposes the Online Harassment Agentic Benchmark, using a synthetic multi-turn harassment dialogue dataset, a multi-agent (harasser, victim) simulation based on repeated game theory, three jailbreak methods targeting memory/planning/fine-tuning, and a hybrid evaluation framework, to test two models: LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and Gemini-2.0-flash. Results show that jailbreak fine-tuning makes harassment almost inevitable, with attack success rate on Llama rising from 57.25–64.19% to 95.78–96.89%, on Gemini from 98.46% to 99.33%, and refusal rates for both models dropping to 1–2%. The most common harmful behaviors are insults (84.9–87.8%, 44.2–50.8% without fine-tuning) and aggressive flaming (81.2–85.1%, 31.5–38.8% without fine-tuning), indicating that guardrails for these behaviors are weaker than for sensitive categories such as sexual harassment or racial harassment.

parts.text: Online harassment often escalates over multiple turns, while existing jailbreak evaluations mostly look at single-turn prompts. Once LLM agents have long-horizon interaction, tool use, and memory, guardrail failures may amplify harassment at higher speed and persistence. The authors evaluate how memory, planning, and fine-tuning affect this kind of abuse.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: The benchmark uses Dolphin3 to expand social media seeds into multi-turn harassment conversations, then simulates a harasser and an avoidant victim with repeated games, up to 10 turns. Attacks compare persona prompting, memory injection, CoT/ReAct, and jailbreak fine-tuning. gpt-4o-mini labels by eight categories, and humans code by dark triad and conflict avoidance.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: LLaMA fine-tuned ASR 95.78–96.89%, without fine-tuning 57.25–64.19%. Qwen3 without fine-tuning 92.50–99.12%. Gemini memory 99.54%, DeepSeek-FT baseline 64.15%. The authors state that Insult and Flaming are the most common.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors note that seed data duplication accounts for 0.83% of the synthetic set, that quality evaluation did not directly use real dialogues, and plan deduplication and additional quality checks. The evaluation covers four model families, at most 10 turns, and human coding for LLaMA-FT and Gemini-FT; the main ASR table does not report the number of dialogues.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: MEEA: Mere Exposure Effect-Driven Confrontational Optimization for LLM Jailbreaking
titleEn: MEEA: A Multi-Turn Jailbreak Attack Framework Based on the Mere Exposure Effect
summary: The researchers propose MEEA (Mere Exposure Effect Attack), a fully automated black-box multi-turn jailbreak framework inspired by the psychological mere exposure effect, which gradually erodes a model's safety alignment constraints through repeated exposure to low-toxicity semantics. The method constructs a semantically progressive prompt chain and uses a simulated annealing strategy combined with semantic similarity, toxicity, and jailbreak effectiveness for optimization. On closed-source and open-source models such as GPT-4, Claude-3.5, and DeepSeek-R1, MEEA consistently achieves higher attack success rates than seven representative baselines, with an average improvement of over 20%. Ablation experiments verify the necessity of annealing optimization and the contextual exposure mechanism. Based on this, the authors argue that LLM safety behavior is dynamic and history-dependent, challenging the assumption of static alignment boundaries, and call for interaction-aware safety evaluation and defense mechanisms.

parts.text: In multi-turn dialogue, the model's effective safety boundary shifts with context, and most jailbreaks are still designed around a static boundary, limiting stability and automation.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: MEEA generates semantically progressive multi-turn prompt chains, uses jailbreak score, toxicity, and semantic similarity as the energy function, accepts suboptimal perturbations via simulated annealing, and rolls back refusals and dead ends.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: On 50 items each from AdvBench and JailbreakBench, the MEEA ASR for five targets is higher than the seven baselines in Table 1, averaging 92.63%; without multi-turn, LLaMA-3.1-8B and GPT-4 are 51.45% and 53.26%.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors state that they only study output-layer failures in text dialogue, that external evaluation may introduce noise, and that the dynamic threshold is heuristic. The experiments do not report the attack model or hyperparameters such as N and τ.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: EquaCode: A Multi-Strategy Jailbreak Approach for Large Language Models via Equation Solving and Code Completion
titleEn: EquaCode: Multi-Strategy Jailbreak via Equation Solving and Code Completion
summary: The researchers propose EquaCode, a multi-strategy jailbreak method implemented through equation solving and code completion, which converts malicious intent into mathematical problems and requires the LLM to solve them with code, using the complexity of cross-domain tasks to shift the model's attention from safety constraints to task completion. Experiments show that the method achieves an average attack success rate of 91.19% on the GPT series and 98.65% on 3 SOTA LLMs, all with only a single query. Ablation experiments show it outperforms using the mathematical equation module or code module alone, and the authors state there is a synergistic effect between the two. This paper is a preprint, and the revised version will be included in AAAI 2026.

parts.text: Aligned LLMs can still be induced to produce harmful outputs by adversarial prompts. The authors believe existing jailbreaks mostly stay within natural language and use only a single strategy, and are therefore insufficient for evaluating robustness.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: EquaCode first splits a malicious query into a subject, a tool, and unknown steps, writes it as a text equation, then places it into a Solver class requiring completion of execution steps. The authors state it does not access parameters and requires a single API request.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: In Table 1, EquaCoder's ASR on GPT-4-turbo is 98.46%, the six-model average is 78.98%, and Llama3.1-405B is 17.88%. The four-model average in Table 2 is 98.99%. In the 50 ablation entries, the full method averages 87.33%, higher than the individual modules.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors point out that the success rate depends on the target model's mathematical and coding capabilities, and plan to increase task forms and automated construction. Experiments cover AdvBench and the models in Tables 1, 2, and 4; Llama-3.3-70B has no ASR. The paper does not report the number of repetitions or the denominator for defense bypass rates.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: VRSA: Jailbreaking Multimodal Large Language Models through Visual Reasoning Sequential Attack
titleEn: VRSA: Jailbreaking Multimodal Large Language Models via Visual Reasoning Sequence Attacks
summary: The researchers propose Visual Reasoning Sequence Attack (VRSA), which decomposes the original harmful text into several order-dependent sub-images, inducing multimodal large models to gradually externalize and aggregate the complete harmful intent. To improve the plausibility of the image sequence scenes, the method introduces Adaptive Scene Refinement to optimize the scenes most relevant to the original harmful query; to maintain semantic continuity of the generated images, it proposes Semantic Coherent Completion, which iteratively rewrites each sub-text with scene context; and it proposes Text-Image Consistency Alignment to maintain semantic consistency. Experiments show that on open-source and closed-source multimodal large models such as GPT-4o and Claude-4.5-Sonnet, VRSA's attack success rate is higher than current state-of-the-art jailbreak methods. Paper number arXiv:2512.05853.

parts.text: MLLM's visual reasoning may be used to induce harmful outputs, but existing jailbreaks mostly target text or single images. The authors state that risks in continuous visual scenes still lack dedicated evaluation.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: VRSA places harmful text into scenes and splits it into sub-texts, generates image sequences through continuity repair and CLIP constraints, by default combines them into a single image, and adds typography and guiding text; the experiments are black-box and do not query the victim model.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Across eight MLLMs, VRSA's average ASR over seven categories is higher than the four baselines, with closed-source models at 52.29%–62.57% (Table 2). For some categories, PRISM or HADES is higher. On the IA subset of GPT-4o, both multi-round and single-round ASR are 66%.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The paper does not specifically discuss limitations. Ablations, sequence length, image form, and multi-turn are all on the Illegal Activities subset with GPT-4o as the target. The paper does not report the number of repetitions, number of queries, review and human agreement, or the thresholds for τ, γ, and similarity.

title: How Many Iterations to Jailbreak? Dynamic Budget Allocation for Multi-Turn LLM Evaluation
titleEn: DAPRO: Dynamic budget allocation for the number of rounds needed for jailbreaks in multi-round LLM evaluation
summary: The paper proposes DAPRO (Dynamic Allocation via PRojected Optimization), a dynamic budget allocation framework for lower bounds on event occurrence times in multi-turn LLM interactions. The authors prove that the method satisfies the expected budget constraint and provides finite-sample coverage guarantees without distributional assumptions, no longer relying on the conditional independence between censoring time and event time required by previous conformal survival methods. Its coverage bound scales with the square root of the average censoring weight and involves only partial samples rather than worst-case weights, making it tighter than prior work. DAPRO can also give unbiased estimates of overall evaluation metrics such as jailbreak rate under finite compute. Across four experiment types—agent task success, LLM jailbreak, harmful content generation, and RAG hallucination—DAPRO's coverage is closer to the nominal level, has lower variance than static baselines, and does not exceed the expected budget.

parts.text: In multi-round evaluation, a successful jailbreak or an agent completing a task may take many rounds to appear, and interactive computation is expensive. The authors aim to estimate time-to-event under an expected budget and provide prediction intervals with coverage guarantees for unseen prompts.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: DAPRO splits calibration samples into three phases: learning a policy, conformal risk control, and deployment. It uses trajectory scores to determine continuation probabilities, reduces the variance of weighted miscoverage under the expected budget, then calibrates quantiles with inverse probability weights, and at test time only looks at the initial prompt.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: On Toxicity, target coverage 90%, per-sample budget 20, the authors claim the average deviation over four models is 1.90× lower than static and variance is 3.32× lower. For Red-Team's Phi-4 Mini, the full event rate is 79.6%, with the lowest estimates being static 66.6% and DAPRO 73.7%.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors note that in the experiments CRC often does not use up the budget, the coverage guarantee depends on calibration and test data being identically distributed, and τ̂ does not vary with the test prompt. The experiments include Toxicity, Red-Team, AutoIF, and an appendix hallucination task, with the target models being the 4 listed in the main text; the main text does not give the original coverage values for each model in Figure 2.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: ChartHal: A Fine-grained Framework Evaluating Hallucination of Large Vision Language Models in Chart Understanding

summary: The researchers propose ChartHal, a fine-grained benchmark for evaluating hallucination in chart understanding by large vision-language models, including a taxonomy of hallucination scenarios and 1,062 human-verified samples. Evaluation shows that current state-of-the-art models exhibit severe hallucination on this benchmark, with GPT-5 and o4-mini achieving only 34.46% and 22.79% accuracy, respectively. Analysis also finds that questions involving information not present in the chart or contradicting it are particularly prone to triggering hallucination. Code and data are publicly released.

parts.text: Chart understanding requires answers to be strictly consistent with the chart, but the authors say existing hallucination evaluations mostly stop at objects and scenes, while chart benchmarks mostly look only at final accuracy, and the intersection of the two has almost never been systematically studied.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: CHART HAL turns the task into free-form chart question answering, crossing descriptive/reasoning/open-ended with irrelevant/inexistent/contradictory/normal into 12 categories. Charts sample 1 or 2 sub-charts from CharXiv, o4-mini generates QA, human verification yields 1,062 items; no hallucination scores 1.

parts.text: The authors note that the charts mainly come from CharXiv's arXiv scientific charts, the taxonomy may not cover real-world questions, and mitigation methods are not systematically compared. Experiments cover 15 LVLMs, 1,062 items, with GPT-4o automatic scoring; the paper does not report agreement between the scoring and human judgment.

title: Text is All You Need for Vision-Language Model Jailbreaking
titleEn: Researchers propose Text-DJ, jailbreaking large vision-language models by exploiting OCR capabilities
summary: The paper proposes Text-DJ, a jailbreak attack that exploits the OCR capability of large vision-language models to bypass existing safety alignment. The method has three steps: decompose a harmful query into multiple semantically related but more harmless sub-queries; select distractor queries least related to the harmful query; input the sub-queries and distractor queries simultaneously to the model as an image grid, with sub-queries placed in the middle of the grid. The authors attribute the attack's success to two factors: converting text prompts into images bypasses standard text filters; and the interference from many unrelated queries prevents the model's safety protocols from linking the scattered sub-queries. The authors claim this method bypasses the safety alignment of current state-of-the-art LVLMs and note the need for defenses designed for fragmented multimodal inputs. Paper number arXiv:2602.00420.

parts.text: LVLM safety checks mostly target explicit text or related images, and white-box attacks requiring gradients cannot be applied to closed-source APIs. The authors want a black-box, model-agnostic jailbreak using only text prompts, exploiting OCR to read in split harmful sub-queries.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Text-DJ uses Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct to split the harmful query into 3 sub-queries, then uses all-MiniLM-L6-v2 to greedily select 9 most unrelated distractor questions, writes them into a 4×3 text image, places sub-queries at positions 6, 8, and 12, and instructs the model to answer these positions.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: On HADES and HEx-PHI, the average ASR of Text-DJ for the six LVLMs is higher than the baselines in the table. On HADES, GPT 4.1 mini achieves 64.27% and Gemini-2.5-Flash achieves 44.00%. The OpenAI refusal rate is 0.00%.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The paper does not specifically discuss method limitations. The conclusion calls for defenses for the OCR module that can resist cross-modal semantic interference. Guardrails and ablations only report on the open-source Qwen3-VL; the number of repetitions for the main experiment's ASR is not reported.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Jailbreaking Safeguarded Text-to-Image Models via Large Language Models
titleEn: Researchers jailbreak text-to-image models with safety guardrails by fine-tuning large language models
summary: The researchers propose a method to jailbreak text-to-image models with safety guardrails by fine-tuning a large language model. The fine-tuned AttackLLM can efficiently generate adversarial prompts without repeatedly querying the target model, unlike other query-based jailbreak attacks. The authors evaluate the method on three unsafe prompt datasets against five safety guardrails, and state that it can effectively bypass the guardrails, outperforming existing no-box attacks, and can assist other query-based attacks. This work has been accepted by EACL 2026 Findings.

parts.text: Protected text-to-image models can still be bypassed by adversarial prompts and generate harmful images such as pornographic content. The authors state that existing jailbreaks often require repeatedly querying the target or surrogate model, and the rewritten results may lack semantics. The goal is to generate adversarial prompts without further querying the target model.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: PromptTune uses Mistral-7B-Instruct to rewrite unsafe prompts. The Judge takes CLIP cosine similarity, filters preference pairs, and then performs SFT or DPO. PT-base is not fine-tuned and only rewrites once.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Three sets of 100 items each, five guardrails. On filtering, PT-base has a higher bypass rate than Ring-A-Bell and MMA; on MACE, its average CLIP score is not higher than no attack. After initializing SneakyPrompt with PT-dpo outputs, online queries decrease in most settings.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors note that the advanced variant requires many queries to the target to build preference data, and that alignment such as MACE remains difficult to bypass in the no-box setting. Experiments use SDXL-Turbo and Mistral-7B-Instruct, with 100 items tested per set; the paper does not report human agreement or the total number of queries for building the data.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: When Persuasion Overrides Truth in Multi-Agent LLM Debates: Introducing a Confidence-Weighted Persuasion Override Rate (CW-POR)
titleEn: The study proposes the CW-POR metric to measure persuasion coverage in multi-agent LLM debates.
summary: The paper proposes Confidence-Weighted Persuasion Override Rate (CW-POR) to measure how often a judge LLM is persuaded by incorrect arguments in multi-agent debate and how confident it is in the wrong option. The study uses a single-round multi-agent debate framework: one LLM-based agent gives the truthful answer from TruthfulQA, another agent argues for the incorrect claim, and the same LLM architecture serves as judge. Experiments cover five open-source LLMs (3B to 14B parameters) and systematically vary agent utterance length (30 to 300 words). Results show that even smaller models can construct persuasive arguments that override truthful answers, often with high confidence. The authors argue this highlights the need for robust calibration and adversarial testing to prevent LLMs from confidently endorsing misinformation.

parts.text: When an LLM both generates and judges, neutral facts and forceful incorrect statements seen in a single round may conflict. The authors aim to measure together how often the judge is persuaded and how confident it is when choosing wrong.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: On the TruthfulQA validation split, the same model family plays the roles of neutral explanation, erroneous defense, and judge. The judge reads both sides randomly and scores 1–5. CW-POR weights incorrect choices using normalized self-assessment multiplied by LLC, with lengths ranging from 30 to 300 words.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Across five 3B–14B models, the authors claim that confident misjudgment is least likely around 90–120 words, with trends diverging after longer lengths. Most models have higher CW-POR on non-adversarial questions; Phi-4 14B still shows high textual confidence when choosing incorrectly. The main text does not include specific percentages.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors propose expanding categories with high CW-POR and few samples, adding limited rebuttals, using judges of different architectures, and applying thresholds or external verification when combined confidence is high. This run covers five models, triangular same-family, single-round; the paper does not report the number of questions or repetitions.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Evolving Skill-Structured Attack Memory Enhances LLM Jailbreaking
titleEn: MemoAttack: Memory-driven black-box jailbreak framework achieves 93.33-96.67% attack success rate on AdvBench
summary: The researchers propose MemoAttack, a memory-driven black-box jailbreak framework that organizes and reuses attack experience through skill-structured memory modeling, lifecycle-driven memory evolution, and posterior-guided contextual memory selection. On AdvBench against three target models, MemoAttack achieves an attack success rate of 93.33-96.67%, outperforming the strongest baseline on each target by 10.00-12.00 percentage points, while reducing the average expansion cost on its own successful targets by 20.2-51.6%. In a sequential evaluation of 400 targets on Qwen3.5, as memory accumulates, the average number of expansion attempts for the last 50 targets drops from 19.74 to 10.92. The paper is marked as under review and belongs to the cs.CR area.

parts.text: Aligned LLMs should refuse harmful requests, but under black-box conditions the attacker only sees outputs, and automatic jailbreaking is sparse and expensive search. Sample-level heuristic search has short-lived experience; cross-sample policy pools lack structured management.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: MemoAttack stores experience as skill memories with templates, evidence, and lifecycle. The controller samples among reuse, mutation, and invention, uses two Beta posteriors for progress and success plus contextual features for Thompson sampling, and shows only a shortlist projection to the attacker.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: On AdvBench, ASR for kimi-k2.5, minimax-M2.1, and qwen3.5 is 95.33%, 96.67%, and 93.33%. Removing memory from Qwen3.5 causes the largest drop; tail expansion count decreases from 19.74 to 10.92.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors note that evaluation is limited to AdvBench text black-box and three targets, does not evaluate Claude Fable 5 or GPT-5.6, and does not systematically study cross-target transfer, hyperparameter sensitivity, or defenses. SD comes from three non-overlapping splits; the paper states that confidence intervals are not computed.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Jailbreaking Large Vision Language Models in Intelligent Transportation Systems
titleEn: The paper proposes jailbreaking LVLMs in intelligent transportation systems using image typographic manipulation and multi-turn prompting
summary: The paper systematically analyzes the vulnerability of large vision-language models (LVLMs) integrated into intelligent transportation systems (ITS) under jailbreak attacks. The authors first construct a traffic-related harmful query dataset based on OpenAI's prohibited categories, then propose a jailbreak attack combining image layout manipulation and multi-turn prompting, and provide a multi-layer response filtering defense technique. Experiments are conducted on multiple open-source and closed-source SOTA LVLMs, using GPT-4 to judge the toxicity scores of generated responses supplemented by human verification, and comparing with existing jailbreak techniques, highlighting the security risks posed by image layout manipulation plus multi-turn prompting to LVLMs in ITS scenarios.

parts.text: LVLMs in ITS read both images and text. The authors believe jailbreaking may elicit responses prohibited by safety policies, citing illegal surveillance, physical harm, ignoring traffic signs, or misclassifying key objects as examples. The paper states that multi-turn jailbreaking of LVLMs and such risks in ITS have not been sufficiently studied.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: The authors used GPT-4 for few-shot generation, then manually filtered to 150 traffic-related harmful queries. The attack extracts keywords, uses Stable Diffusion to generate object images, and turns harmful text into image captions, then uses a fixed three-round prompt to progressively request harmful explanations. The defense first matches phrases, then a classifier decides whether to reject or allow.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: GPT-4-evaluated Turn3 ASR for LLaVa-1.6, Qwen-2, and GPT-4o-mini is 92.67%, 84.12%, and 74.67%. The authors state this is higher than FigStep and MM-SafetyBench on the two open-source models. After filtering, it is 5.31%, 25.33%, and 30.67%.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors state that GPT-4's detection of subtle harmful content still needs development, and plan to add baselines, datasets, and defenses, as well as use query optimization to generate multi-turn prompts, then evaluate commercial and inference-oriented LVLMs. The experiments are text toxicity scores for 3 models and 150 queries; the paper does not report the classifier model or number of repetitions.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: The Tower of Babel Revisited: Multilingual Jailbreak Prompts on Closed-Source Large Language Models
titleEn: Attack evaluation of multilingual jailbreak prompts against closed-source large language models: GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, Gemini-1.5-Pro, and Qwen-Max
summary: A study tested 32 jailbreak attacks on GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, Gemini-1.5-Pro, and Qwen-Max with 38,400 trials across six safety content categories in Chinese and English, measuring performance by attack success rate (ASR). Results show Qwen-Max is most easily compromised and GPT-4o has the strongest defenses; the ASR for Chinese prompts is consistently higher than English, and the newly proposed Two-Sides attack is most effective on all models. The authors state this highlights the urgent need for language-aware alignment and cross-lingual defenses.

parts.text: Commercial closed-source models are deployed via APIs, but security research mostly focuses on open-source models and English scenarios. The authors aim to compare GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, Gemini-1.5-Pro, and Qwen-Max in terms of defenses against Chinese-English jailbreak prompts, and how prompt structure changes the bypass rate.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Self-built 32 forbidden questions translated into Chinese and English, using role setting, sandwich wrapping, pro-con argumentation, and format guidance to compose jailbreak prompts, then ablating each component. Each variant repeated 25 times, two annotators plus a third arbitrator, only Success counted in ASR.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Among 38,400 outputs, under Full-Attack the Chinese ASR of Qwen-Max is 0.8925 and the English ASR of GPT-4o is 0.3219 (Table 2). The authors state that Chinese prompts are generally higher, and that two-sided argumentation is the most effective component; the ASR for attack-only prompts is near zero.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors point out that static one-time evaluation cannot keep up with model updates and that only Chinese and English are covered. Future plans include interpretable white-box attacks, human-machine collaborative annotation, and expanding Chinese safety benchmarks. The experiment covered four closed-source APIs, six categories with 32 questions, six variants, 25 repetitions per variant, with manual annotation and no agreement scores calculated.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: SafeScientist: Toward Risk-Aware Scientific Discoveries by LLM Agents
titleEn: SafeScientist: Making LLM agents' scientific discoveries risk-aware
summary: The researchers propose an AI scientist framework called SafeScientist that proactively refuses ethically inappropriate or high-risk tasks and integrates prompt monitoring, agent collaboration monitoring, tool-use monitoring, and ethics review components. The accompanying benchmark SciSafetyBench covers 240 high-risk scientific tasks across 6 domains, 30 scientific tools, and 120 tool-related risk tasks. Experiments show its safety performance improves by 35% over traditional AI scientist frameworks without harming research output quality, and the robustness of the safety pipeline is verified under multiple adversarial attacks.

parts.text: Research LLM agents may execute high-risk or unethical tasks. The authors believe that existing safety work rarely covers multi-agent research pipelines, so they propose SafeScientist and evaluate it with SciSafetyBench.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: On Tiny Scientist, add four layers of monitoring: LLaMA-Guard-3-8B and SafeChecker fusion refusal, discussion monitoring, tool monitoring, and ethics review. The benchmark contains 240 tasks, 30 tools, 120 tool scenarios, and is tested with query injection and malicious agents.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: On 20 Biology questions, SafeChecker has safety score 4.83 and refusal rate 90% (Table 2). Fuse's average refusal rate is 78.70% (Table 3). Under malicious tool instructions, safety rates range from 5.8% to 47.5% (Table 5). Refusal is scored 5, and its quality score is not included.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors note that off-the-shelf LLM modules are separate and tool evaluation is only simulated, and they plan end-to-end architectures, multimodal or embodied evaluation, and expanded benchmarks and real-time defenses. The main comparison is 20 questions on Biology; the Table 4 note states the values are placeholders.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Prompt-in-Content Attacks: Exploiting Uploaded Inputs to Hijack LLM Behavior
titleEn: Prompt-in-Content attacks: hijacking LLM behavior using uploaded input
summary: The paper proposes a new class of attack called prompt in content injection, which embeds adversarial instructions in seemingly benign uploaded documents or pasted text. After the LLM processes them, it can generate biased summaries, fabricated claims, or misleading advice, without user awareness and without the system being compromised. The authors verified the feasibility of the attack on multiple mainstream platforms, analyzed its root cause as insufficient prompt concatenation and input isolation, and discussed mitigation strategies.

parts.text: Commercial LLMs often concatenate the uploaded document and the user query into the same prompt. A third party can embed instructions in a seemingly normal file, and when the user performs an ordinary task such as summarization, the model may rewrite, refuse, or deflect the output without the user's knowledge.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: The authors define the prompt-in-content attack: the attacker pre-writes a single natural-language instruction in the middle of a document, without touching the model interface or using jailbreaks. The four goal types are task suppression, output replacement, behavior redirection, and framework manipulation. The evaluation uploads .docx files on the default web interfaces of seven services and observes the outputs.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: The authors state that most platforms execute embedded instructions. Table 1: Grok 3, DeepSeek R1, and Kimi were successful across all four types; Claude Sonnet4 and ChatGPT 4o blocked all four types. Grok 3 also placed the previously mentioned password into a redirect link (Figure 5).
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors limited themselves to single-turn public web interfaces and did not examine multi-turn persistence, long-term memory leakage, or account-linked poisoning; the exfiltration test was in a controlled environment and did not use real user data. The evaluation covered seven web services with a single mid-document instruction in .docx files, did not report sample size or number of repetitions, and did not experimentally evaluate the defense recommendations in Section 5.2.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Multi-turn Jailbreaking Attack in Multi-Modal Large Language Models
titleEn: Multi-turn jailbreak attacks on multimodal large language models and FragGuard defense
summary: The paper proposes the MJAD-MLLMs framework, systematically analyzing multi-turn jailbreak attacks and multi-LLM-based defense techniques for multimodal large language models (MLLMs). The authors design a new multi-turn jailbreak attack that exploits model vulnerabilities under multi-turn prompts, and propose a fragment optimization and multi-LLM defense mechanism, FragGuard, to mitigate such attacks. The study evaluates the attack and defense effectiveness on multiple SOTA open-source and closed-source MLLMs and benchmark datasets, and compares with existing techniques.

parts.text: The basic guardrails of MLLMs may be bypassed by multi-turn multimodal prompts. Multi-turn jailbreak research exists on the text side, but systematic analysis is lacking on the MLLM side; the authors believe existing defenses may be insufficient against multi-turn jailbreaks.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: The framework MJAD-MLLMs induces jailbreak through three rounds of dialogue and bottom-aligned images. FragGuard splits responses at 400 tokens, uses o1, Gemini-2.5-Flash-lite, and LLaMa-3 (70B) to take the maximum toxicity score, and if it exceeds the threshold, it changes to a safe refusal.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: LLaVa-7B and GPT-4o have Turn3 ASR of 91.50% and 77.31% (Table 1). After FragGuard, they are 0.96% and 8.08% (Table 3). The authors state that Gemini-2.0-Flash has an ASR of 82.3%.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors plan to automatically generate adversarial prompts and analyze defenses for commercial and reasoning MLLMs and automated attacks. Experiments use MM-SafetyBench with 40 items per category; Table 3 only includes two models. The paper does not report threshold τ and repetition count.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: What Output-Only Review Cannot Verify: Study Contracts for Research Agents
titleEn: What output-only review cannot verify: a research contract for research agents
summary: The research proposes a "research contract" mechanism that binds experiment selection, execution obligations, and conclusion scope to recorded execution evidence, in order to distinguish contract-level verification from scientific truth. In eight groups of self-made clean/mutation paired diagnostics, the deterministic checker applies registered fault-specific rules to approved and executed objects and detects all eight registered mutations; among eighteen review aliases and 144 mutation evaluation cases, 104 are flagged as defective, with the rest being 32 abstentions and 8 termination failures, and no explicit "clean" determination on mutation cases. The authors state that this result characterizes a development environment with deliberate information asymmetry and does not constitute a comparison of validator quality or agent reward hacking.

parts.text: Research on agent improvement loops often uses task completion, artifacts, or manuscript review as rewards. These signals do not necessarily encode the relationship between approved research and actual execution, and looking only at outputs may not verify the contractual relative methodological qualifications.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: The authors treat the approved research contract as the environment, checking versioned bindings, expected run denominators, typed claim promotion, and out-of-band human gates. The diagnosis uses eight pairs of self-authored packages: the deterministic checker holds approved objects and applies fault-specific rules, while eighteen aliases filter packages by metadata only.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: The checker blocks 8/8 registered mutations and falsely blocks 0/8. Eighteen aliases give 104 fault flags and 0 explicit clean judgments across 144 mutation cases; intra-package contradiction classes are 16/18 to 18/18, and the two missing-fault classes are 2/18 and 1/18. The authors call this deliberate information asymmetry, not a validator quality comparison.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: Information cross-checking, legitimate adaptation control, and closed-loop evaluation have not been run, so the advantage cannot be attributed to the checker itself. The authors state this is not reward hacking; the fixtures and labels are self-authored with no held-out calibration. Coverage is 18 unfixed aliases and eight pairs of packages; the paper does not report agreement with humans.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Controlling risks of AI in chemical science with agents
titleEn: Controlling AI risks in chemical science with agents: the SciGuard guardrail and the SciMT benchmark
summary: The paper proposes an agent-based guardrail, SciGuard, that uses large language models, tools, and external knowledge to assess and control risks in scientific AI interactions, and provides a benchmark, SciMT, that measures both safety and usability. SciGuard achieves SOTA harmlessness scores on red-teaming test queries while maintaining high performance on benign tasks without sacrificing scientific knowledge. The authors first list real cases of AI misuse in chemical science and call for continued research and dialogue to ensure safe deployment of AI in science.

parts.text: Synthesis planning, toxicity prediction, and language models in chemical science could be used to propose harmful substances, circumvent regulations, or spread dangerous information. The authors argue that existing safety mechanisms are often insufficient, requiring contextual control without modifying the underlying models.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: SciGuard uses an LLM as an external mediator, with principles, guidelines, molecular and regulatory memory, scientific tools, and RAG for iterative planning, then decides whether to answer, ask for clarification, or refuse. SciMT uses four parts—red teaming, scientific information, legislation, and jailbreak—to evaluate both safety and utility.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: In Table 1, SciGuard (GPT-4) has Redteam 5.00, ScienceInfo 90.00, and Jailbreak 5.00. The Mixtral version has Jailbreak 3.43, which is not the highest among the models. The authors state there are improvements over the base models.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The conclusion states that inputs may be ambiguous or deceptive, that complex adversarial and misclassification cases remain to be studied, and that SciMT does not exhaust chemical risks. The evaluation includes 12 systems in Table 1, as well as a benign set, an MMLU sample, and WMDP-Chem. The paper does not report human agreement correlation coefficients.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: MARGIN: Runtime Confidence Calibration for Multi-Agent Foundation Model Coordination
titleEn: MARGIN: Runtime Confidence Calibration for Multi-Agent Foundation Model Coordination
summary: The paper proposes MARGIN (Multi-Agent Runtime Grading via Incremental Normalisation), a runtime calibration method that learns model-specific confidence corrections from observed answer outcomes without retraining models or a held-out calibration set. In code generation, question answering, and math evaluations on an 18-model pool and a 9-model subset, MARGIN achieved lower post-transfer expected calibration error than all five online calibration baselines on two code generation transfers, and lower than four on the question answering transfer. In code generation coordination experiments, calibration improved answer selection accuracy on two benchmarks by 4.3 and 14.0 percentage points, respectively.

parts.text: The coordinator needs to compare answers from heterogeneous base models using self-reported confidence; the same score means different things across models, and after the task distribution changes the old correction may also no longer apply. The authors argue this becomes a coordination problem, not just a single-model diagnostic.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Within each model's confidence bands, MARGIN tracks accuracy and self-reported confidence with an EWMA, corrects scores by their ratio, and shrinks sparse bands toward that model's overall ratio. The corrected scores serve as voting weights for the answers already obtained. No retraining, no access to internal state, no separate calibration set, but it depends on subsequent correctness feedback.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: After two code transfers, nine-cloud MARGIN achieves ECE of 12.99 and 11.89, lower than the five online baselines; MMLU-shift is 2.85, inconclusive compared with online Platt. The 18-model cold-start selection accuracy improves by 4.32 and 13.98 percentage points on MBPP and BCB.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors state that applicability depends on correctness feedback; verifying only the selected answerer harms calibration; generalization is limited by the archived queue and mutation transfer, and gradual drift was not tested. The experiments use an 18-model pool and a nine-cloud subset; question answering and math only do calibration, not voting.
parts.label: Limitations and future work
